checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-016: Does parse_deposit_requests enforce two-layer deposit event filtering?

audit_items.state_context: processingLock sync.RWMutex — only RLock acquired, WLock never called. lastReceivedMerkleIndex int64 — written under read lock. depositTrie — modified under read lock.
audit_items.reasoning: Two concrete vulnerabilities found: (1) processingLock sync.RWMutex is only ever acquired as RLock in ProcessLog/ProcessDepositLog. The write lock (Lock()) is never called anywhere in the execution package. This makes the lastReceivedMerkleIndex deduplication non-atomic: concurrent goroutines can both pass the index <= lastReceivedMerkleIndex guard under concurrent read locks, then both attempt to write to shared trie state, causing double-insertion or state inconsistency. (2) The EIP-6110 path (ProcessDepositRequests/processDepositRequest) has no per-request index monotonicity check after DepositRequestsStartIndex is set — a duplicate or replayed DepositRequest is appended to pending_deposits unchecked. Additionally, ProcessLog accesses depositLog.Topics[0] without a len(Topics) guard, risking panic on empty Topics slice.

phase1.summary: Critical state anomaly: processingLock.RLock() used exclusively for a function that performs writes to shared state (lastReceivedMerkleIndex, depositTrie). Write lock is never acquired anywhere in the package. EIP-6110 path missing sequential index validation.
anomalies: processingLock is sync.RWMutex but only RLock/RUnlock called — writes to lastReceivedMerkleIndex and depositTrie occur under read lock
Topics[0] accessed without len(depositLog.Topics) > 0 guard — potential index-out-of-bounds panic
uint64 to int64 cast for merkle index: overflow at values > math.MaxInt64 wraps to negative, bypasses <= check
processDepositRequest: no index monotonicity check after DepositRequestsStartIndex is initialized

phase2.summary: Counterexample found for race condition: two goroutines concurrently calling ProcessLog with same deposit log can both pass deduplication guard under read locks.
counterexamples: Goroutines G1 and G2 both call ProcessLog with merkleTreeIndex=N while lastReceivedMerkleIndex=N-1. Both acquire RLock concurrently. Both evaluate N <= N-1 as false. Both pass the guard. Race on lastReceivedMerkleIndex and depositTrie follows.
Attacker submits same DepositRequest twice via EL in consecutive blocks. Both appended to pending_deposits without index check. Potential double-deposit credit on beacon chain.

phase2_5.summary: Attack surfaces confirmed: permissionless deposit contract enables crafted logs; engine API interaction allows duplicate DepositRequests from compromised EL.
findings: ETH1 log deduplication race exploitable via concurrent block processing
EIP-6110 replay window between blocks for duplicate deposit requests

phase3.summary: Invariant violations confirmed: Layer 2 ETH1 deduplication is non-atomic (RLock instead of WLock). EIP-6110 path has no Layer 2 equivalent.

phase3_5.summary: Fix: Change processingLock.RLock() to processingLock.Lock() in ProcessLog. Add len(depositLog.Topics) > 0 guard. Add sequential index check in processDepositRequest. Add int64 overflow check before cast.
attack_scenarios: Concurrent beacon node block processing triggers two goroutines to process same deposit log simultaneously, bypassing deduplication under read locks, resulting in double trie insertion.
Compromised/malicious EL sends duplicate DepositRequest in two consecutive Electra blocks; both appended to pending_deposits, potentially crediting a validator twice.

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-016: Does extract_deposit_data validate 576-byte length and offsets?

audit_items.state_context: Caller ProcessDepositLog uses: binary.LittleEndian.Uint64(merkleTreeIndex) — panics if len(merkleTreeIndex) < 8. bytesutil.FromBytes8(amount) — silently returns 0 if amount < 8 bytes.
audit_items.reasoning: UnpackDepositLogData performs no explicit validation of the 576-byte total ABI-encoded length, nor any post-decode field length validation. The Ethereum deposit contract accepts arbitrary-length bytes fields from any permissionless account. If the ABI decoder returns an 'index' field shorter than 8 bytes (theoretically possible with malformed/non-standard encoding), the subsequent call to binary.LittleEndian.Uint64(merkleTreeIndex) in ProcessDepositLog will panic due to insufficient slice length. The unsafe type assertions (unpackedLogs[N].([]byte)) will also panic if the ABI decoder returns an unexpected type. No len(unpackedLogs) check ensures the expected 5 elements are present.

phase1.summary: No explicit 576-byte length check before Unpack. No post-decode field length validation (pubkey=48, withdrawalCredentials=32, amount=8, signature=96, index=8). Unsafe type assertions on ABI decoder output. ABI string re-parsed on every call (performance concern).
anomalies: Unsafe type assertions: unpackedLogs[0].([]byte) panics if type unexpected
No post-decode field length validation for any of the 5 fields
Caller uses binary.LittleEndian.Uint64(index) without len check — panics if len(index) < 8

phase2.summary: Counterexample: permissionless deposit contract interaction with crafted short 'index' field triggers panic in ProcessDepositLog via binary.LittleEndian.Uint64.
counterexamples: Attacker calls deposit contract with index encoded as <8 bytes. ABI decoder returns index as []byte of length <8. ProcessDepositLog calls binary.LittleEndian.Uint64(merkleTreeIndex) which panics (runtime: slice bounds out of range). Result: beacon node goroutine crash or panic recovery depending on Go runtime behavior.
If go-ethereum ABI Unpack returns fewer than 5 elements for malformed data, unpackedLogs[4].([]byte) panics with index out of range.

phase2_5.summary: Attack requires a real Ethereum transaction to the deposit contract with crafted field lengths — possible for any account with ETH. Severity is remotely-triggerable DoS against beacon node deposit processing.
findings: Permissionless attack vector: any ETH holder can submit a deposit with non-standard field lengths
Go's ABI decoder may not reject all field-length anomalies depending on go-ethereum version

phase3.summary: Property violated: no 576-byte total length check exists. No per-field length validation post-decode. The go-ethereum ABI library provides some defense but is not a substitute for explicit validation.

phase3_5.summary: Fix: Add len(data) == 576 (or >= minimum) check before Unpack. After Unpack, validate: len(pubkey)==48, len(withdrawalCredentials)==32, len(amount)==8, len(signature)==96, len(index)==8. Use safe type assertions with ok checks.
attack_scenarios: Permissionless deposit contract call with 'index' field shorter than 8 bytes causes binary.LittleEndian.Uint64 panic in ProcessDepositLog, potentially crashing the deposit processing goroutine.
Malformed ABI encoding bypassing go-ethereum's decoder causing unexpected types in unpackedLogs, triggering type assertion panics.

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-017: Is compute_requests_hash deterministic across all clients?

audit_items.state_context: EncodeExecutionRequests serializes Deposits(0), Withdrawals(1), Consolidations(2) in fixed iota order. Empty request lists are omitted. SSZ marshaling is deterministic. RequestsHash computed by EL, not Prysm.
audit_items.reasoning: Prysm correctly delegates RequestsHash computation to the execution layer per EIP-7685 architecture. EncodeExecutionRequests is a pure deterministic function: same ExecutionRequests struct always produces same flattenedRequests byte slice (fixed type ordering via Go iota constants, deterministic SSZ marshaling, empty lists omitted per spec). The nil requests guard in notifyNewPayload correctly rejects nil ExecutionRequests for Electra blocks. No Prysm-side non-determinism found. Cross-client hash agreement is enforced by the EL per the engine API spec, not by CL consensus clients.

phase1.summary: Prysm does not compute RequestsHash. EncodeExecutionRequests uses fixed iota ordering (Deposits=0, Withdrawals=1, Consolidations=2) with SSZ marshaling. Nil guard present for Electra blocks. RequestsHash verification delegated to EL via engine_newPayloadV4.

phase2.summary: No counterexample to determinism found. EncodeExecutionRequests is a pure function with no state dependencies. Same input always produces same output.

phase2_5.summary: Cross-client concern: if another CL emits empty request type bytes while Prysm omits them, EL-computed hashes would differ. This is a spec conformance question outside Prysm's control.
findings: Potential cross-client divergence on empty request type handling — but this is a spec-level concern, not a Prysm bug

phase3.summary: Invariant holds within Prysm: same ExecutionRequests → same serialization → same RequestsHash from EL. Architecture correctly follows EIP-7685.

phase3_5.summary: No exploitable attack scenario within Prysm's implementation. Cross-client divergence would be a spec interpretation issue, not a code bug.
